notes.front: What is the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework?
notes.back: Google’s set of recommendations for designing and operating a cloud topology that is secure, efficient, resilient, high-performing, cost-effective and sustainable.
notes.explanation: It is written for architects, developers, administrators and other cloud practitioners, so it is a shared reference rather than a product.
notes.example: Like a building code for cloud designs, but advisory: it recommends practices instead of enforcing them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”
notes.evidence: The Well-Architected Framework provides recommendations to help architects, developers, administrators, and other cloud practitioners design and operate a cloud topology that's secure, efficient, resilient, high-performing, cost-effective, and sustainable.

notes.front: What does the zero trust principle ask of you, in the framework’s security pillar?
notes.back: A never trust, always verify approach: access to resources is granted based on continuous verification of trust.
notes.explanation: Implementing zero trust is one of the core principles that group the security pillar’s recommendations.
notes.example: Like a building where your badge is checked at every door, not just once at the front gate.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement zero trust: Use a never trust, always verify approach, where access to resources is granted based on continuous verification of trust.

notes.front: What is shift-left security, in the framework’s security pillar?
notes.back: Implementing security controls early in the software development lifecycle, so defects are avoided before changes are made.
notes.explanation: The same principle also asks you to detect and fix security bugs early, fast and reliably once changes are committed.
notes.example: Like scanning a container image for known vulnerabilities in the build pipeline, instead of discovering them after release.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement shift-left security: Implement security controls early in the software development lifecycle. Avoid security defects before system changes are made.

notes.front: How does the cost optimisation pillar relate to FinOps?
notes.back: Its core principles are closely aligned with the core tenets of cloud FinOps.
notes.explanation: The pillar adds that FinOps is relevant to any organisation, regardless of its size or cloud maturity.
notes.example: Like a household budget practice applied to cloud bills, with engineers as well as finance seeing what their choices cost.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: These principles are closely aligned with the core tenets of cloud FinOps. FinOps is relevant to any organization, regardless of its size or maturity in the cloud.

notes.front: What is the AI and ML perspective of the Well-Architected Framework?
notes.back: A cross-pillar view of technology-specific recommendations for AI and ML workloads.
notes.explanation: It gathers AI- and ML-specific principles and recommendations for the framework’s pillars in one place.
notes.example: Like a subject-specific appendix to a general handbook: the same chapters, but read through the lens of model training and serving.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Cross-pillar perspectives”
notes.evidence: AI and ML A cross-pillar view of technology-specific recommendations for AI and ML workloads.

notes.front: Is the Well-Architected Framework only for applications built for the cloud?
notes.back: No. It also applies to workloads migrated from on-premises, hybrid cloud deployments and multi-cloud environments.
notes.explanation: Its scope is any Google Cloud topology, whatever route the workload took to get there.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”
notes.evidence: The Well-Architected Framework is relevant to applications built for the cloud and for workloads migrated from on-premises to Google Cloud, hybrid cloud deployments, and multi-cloud environments.

notes.front: The recommendations in the Well-Architected Framework are organised into pillars and {{c1::cross-pillar perspectives}}.
notes.explanation: Pillars cover focus areas; perspectives cut across them for one technology, domain or sector.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”
notes.evidence: The recommendations in the Well-Architected Framework are organized into pillars and cross-pillar perspectives

notes.front: What does a pillar of the Well-Architected Framework provide?
notes.back: Principles and recommendations for one non-functional focus area.
notes.explanation: The six focus areas are security, reliability, performance, cost, operations and sustainability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”
notes.evidence: A pillar in the Well-Architected Framework provides principles and recommendations for a specific non-functional focus area: security, reliability, performance, cost, operations, or sustainability.

notes.front: The Well-Architected Framework has {{c1::six}} pillars.
notes.explanation: Operational excellence; security, privacy and compliance; reliability; cost optimisation; performance optimisation; sustainability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: security, reliability, performance, cost, operations, or sustainability.

notes.front: Which pillar is about efficiently deploying, operating, monitoring and managing your cloud workloads?
notes.explanation: It is the framework’s pillar for running workloads day to day, as opposed to how they are secured or priced.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Operational excellence Efficiently deploy, operate, monitor, and manage your cloud workloads.

notes.front: What is the full name of the Well-Architected Framework’s security pillar?
notes.explanation: The pillar also covers designing for privacy and aligning with regulatory requirements and standards, not only protecting data and workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Security, privacy, and compliance Maximize the security of your data and workloads in the cloud, design for privacy, and align with regulatory requirements and standards.

notes.front: Which pillar is about designing and operating resilient, highly available workloads?
notes.explanation: Resilient and highly available workloads are the pillar’s stated aim.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Reliability Design and operate resilient and highly available workloads in the cloud.

notes.front: Which pillar aims to maximise the business value of your investment in Google Cloud?
notes.explanation: The aim is framed as business value, not simply spending less.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Cost optimization Maximize the business value of your investment in Google Cloud.

notes.front: Which pillar is about designing and tuning cloud resources for optimal performance?
notes.explanation: It concerns speed and efficiency of resources, while reliability concerns staying available.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Performance optimization Design and tune your cloud resources for optimal performance.

notes.front: Which pillar is about building and managing cloud workloads that are environmentally sustainable?
notes.explanation: It is the pillar that looks at energy and environmental impact rather than money or speed.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Sustainability Build and manage cloud workloads that are environmentally sustainable.

notes.front: What is a perspective in the Well-Architected Framework?
notes.back: A cross-pillar view of recommendations for a specific technology, domain or sector.
notes.explanation: Its recommendations align with the general principles and recommendations in the pillars.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”
notes.evidence: A perspective in the Well-Architected Framework is a cross-pillar view of recommendations for a specific technology, domain, or sector. The recommendations in a perspective align with the general principles and recommendations in the pillars.

notes.front: Besides AI and ML, which cross-pillar perspective does the Well-Architected Framework list?
notes.explanation: It gives a cross-pillar view of recommendations for financial services workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Cross-pillar perspectives”
notes.evidence: Financial services A cross-pillar view of recommendations for FS workloads.

notes.front: The financial services perspective recommends a disaster recovery strategy that meets data residency rules. Which reliability principle does that align with?
notes.explanation: Data residency limits the choice of failover region, which in turn shapes the recovery objectives.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”
notes.evidence: This FS-specific recommendation aligns with the reliability pillar's principle about realistic targets, because the data residency requirements influence the choice of failover region and, consequently, the recovery objectives.

notes.front: For which pillars does the AI and ML perspective publish its own pages?
notes.back: Operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimisation and performance optimisation.
notes.explanation: The perspective page lists one AI and ML page per pillar for these five.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: AI and ML perspective”, “Well-Architected Framework: AI and ML perspective”
notes.evidence: AI and ML perspective: Operational excellence AI and ML perspective: Security AI and ML perspective: Reliability AI and ML perspective: Cost optimization AI and ML perspective: Performance optimization

notes.front: Which core principle of the framework starts from the idea that no system is static?
notes.explanation: It asks for a process that lets teams regularly deliver small changes and get fast feedback on them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Design for change”
notes.evidence: No system is static. The needs of its users, the goals of the team that builds the system, and the system itself are constantly changing. With the need for change in mind, build a development and production process that enables teams to regularly deliver small changes and get fast feedback on those changes.

notes.front: Which core principle warns that a lack of documentation can be a major obstacle when you move workloads to the cloud?
notes.explanation: Documentation matters most for correctly visualising the architecture of current deployments.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Document your architecture”
notes.evidence: When you start to move your workloads to the cloud or build your applications, lack of documentation about the system can be a major obstacle. Documentation is especially important for correctly visualizing the architecture of your current deployments.

notes.front: According to the framework, is quality documentation achieved by producing a set amount of it?
notes.back: No. It depends on how clear and useful the content is and how it is maintained as the system changes.
notes.explanation: The principle measures documentation by clarity, usefulness and upkeep rather than volume.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Document your architecture”
notes.evidence: Quality documentation isn't achieved by producing a specific amount of documentation, but by how clear content is, how useful it is, and how it's maintained as the system changes.

notes.front: Which core principle recommends using fully managed services where feasible?
notes.back: Simplify your design and use fully managed services.
notes.explanation: Managed services minimise the risk, time and effort of managing and maintaining baseline systems.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Simplify your design and use fully managed services”
notes.evidence: Where feasible, use fully managed services to minimize the risks, time, and effort associated with managing and maintaining baseline systems.

notes.front: For a new workload, how does the framework say you should start?
notes.back: Start simple, establish a minimum viable product and resist the urge to over-engineer.
notes.explanation: You can then find exceptional use cases, iterate and improve the system over time.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Simplify your design and use fully managed services”
notes.evidence: If you're developing new workloads, then start simple, establish a minimal viable product (MVP), and resist the urge to over-engineer.

notes.front: Which core principle separates applications and service components into smaller components that can operate independently?
notes.explanation: Splitting a monolithic application stack into individual service components is the framework’s example of decoupling.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Decouple your architecture”
notes.evidence: Decoupling is a technique that's used to separate your applications and service components into smaller components that can operate independently.

notes.front: What are two kinds of flexibility that a decoupled architecture gives you?
notes.back: Any two of: independent upgrades; specific security controls; reliability goals per subsystem; health monitoring; fine control of performance and cost.
notes.explanation: Each component can then be managed on its own terms rather than as part of one block.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Decouple your architecture”
notes.evidence: A decoupled architecture gives you increased flexibility to do the following: Apply independent upgrades. Enforce specific security controls. Establish reliability goals for each subsystem. Monitor health. Granularly control performance and cost parameters.

notes.front: According to the framework, what two qualities can a stateless architecture increase?
notes.explanation: Stateless applications scale up quickly with minimal boot dependencies and withstand hard restarts.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Use a stateless architecture”
notes.evidence: A stateless architecture can increase both the reliability and scalability of your applications.

notes.front: How does a stateful application differ from a stateless one, according to the framework?
notes.back: A stateful one relies on dependencies such as local caching; a stateless one uses shared storage or cached services instead.
notes.explanation: Stateful applications often need extra mechanisms to capture progress and restart gracefully.
notes.contrast: Stateless: can withstand hard restarts, with lower downtime.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Use a stateless architecture”
notes.evidence: Stateful applications rely on various dependencies to perform tasks, such as local caching of data. Stateful applications often require additional mechanisms to capture progress and restart gracefully. Stateless applications can perform tasks without significant local dependencies by using shared storage or cached services.

notes.front: A web tier keeps each user’s shopping basket in the memory of the virtual machine that served them, so a restart loses baskets and new instances take long to warm up. Which framework core principle does this design break?
notes.choices:
A) Document your architecture
B) Use a stateless architecture
C) Design for change
D) Simplify your design and use fully managed services
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns records of the design, not where session data lives. C concerns delivering small changes with fast feedback. D concerns managed services and avoiding over-engineering; the lost baskets come from local state.
notes.explanation: Keeping state in shared storage or a cache lets instances restart hard and scale up quickly.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Use a stateless architecture”
notes.evidence: Stateless applications can perform tasks without significant local dependencies by using shared storage or cached services. A stateless architecture enables your applications to scale up quickly with minimum boot dependencies.

notes.front: One team wants to upgrade its payment code without redeploying the whole product, and to set a stricter reliability goal for payments than for the rest. Which core principle supports this?
notes.choices:
A) Decouple your architecture
B) Use a stateless architecture
C) Document your architecture
D) Design for change
notes.choicesExplained: B is about where state is kept, not about separating components. C gives shared language and context but does not separate code paths. D is about regular small changes; it does not by itself let one part upgrade alone.
notes.explanation: Independent upgrades and per-subsystem reliability goals are both among the flexibilities a decoupled architecture gives.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Decouple your architecture”
notes.evidence: A decoupled architecture gives you increased flexibility to do the following: Apply independent upgrades. Enforce specific security controls. Establish reliability goals for each subsystem.

notes.front: Which operational excellence principle is about defining service level objectives and performing monitoring, performance testing and capacity planning?
notes.back: Ensure operational readiness and performance using CloudOps.
notes.explanation: Its aim is that cloud solutions meet their operational and performance requirements.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Ensure operational readiness and performance using CloudOps: Ensure that cloud solutions meet operational and performance requirements by defining service level objectives (SLOs) and by performing comprehensive monitoring, performance testing, and capacity planning.

notes.front: Which operational excellence principle aims to minimise the impact of incidents and prevent their recurrence?
notes.explanation: It relies on observability, clear incident response procedures, thorough retrospectives and preventive measures.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Manage incidents and problems: Minimize the impact of cloud incidents and prevent recurrence through comprehensive observability, clear incident response procedures, thorough retrospectives, and preventive measures.

notes.front: Which operational excellence principle names right-sizing, autoscaling and cost monitoring tools as its strategies?
notes.explanation: This is where the operations pillar overlaps with cost: it is about using resources efficiently.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Manage and optimize cloud resources: Optimize and manage cloud resources through strategies like right-sizing, autoscaling, and by using effective cost monitoring tools.

notes.front: Which operational excellence principle aims to streamline change management and relieve the burden of manual labour?
notes.explanation: The principle pairs automation of processes with streamlined change management.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Automate and manage change: Automate processes, streamline change management, and alleviate the burden of manual labor.

notes.front: Which operational excellence principle focuses on ongoing enhancements and new solutions to stay competitive?
notes.explanation: It is the pillar’s forward-looking principle, alongside the four about running and changing workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Continuously improve and innovate: Focus on ongoing enhancements and the introduction of new solutions to stay competitive.

notes.front: In the operational excellence pillar, what does automation help to eliminate?
notes.explanation: Automation also streamlines repetitive tasks and builds guardrails around them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”
notes.evidence: Automation helps to eliminate toil. It also streamlines and builds guardrails around repetitive tasks.

notes.front: The same storage outage has hit a service three times this quarter. Each time the team restored service quickly but held no review. Which operational excellence principle are they neglecting?
notes.choices:
A) Automate and manage change
B) Manage and optimise cloud resources
C) Continuously improve and innovate
D) Manage incidents and problems
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns automating processes and change management. B concerns right-sizing, autoscaling and cost tools. C concerns new solutions to stay competitive; the gap here is learning from repeat incidents.
notes.explanation: That principle aims to prevent recurrence through thorough retrospectives and preventive measures, not only fast recovery.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Manage incidents and problems: Minimize the impact of cloud incidents and prevent recurrence through comprehensive observability, clear incident response procedures, thorough retrospectives, and preventive measures.

notes.front: An operations lead finds dozens of virtual machines running at 5% utilisation and wants to shrink them and add autoscaling. Which operational excellence principle is she applying?
notes.back: A: Manage and optimise cloud resources.
notes.choices:
A) Manage and optimise cloud resources
B) Ensure operational readiness and performance using CloudOps
C) Manage incidents and problems
D) Continuously improve and innovate
notes.choicesExplained: B is about service level objectives, monitoring, testing and capacity planning. C is about incidents and their recurrence. D is about new solutions and staying competitive.
notes.explanation: Right-sizing and autoscaling are the strategies this principle names.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Manage and optimize cloud resources: Optimize and manage cloud resources through strategies like right-sizing, autoscaling, and by using effective cost monitoring tools.

notes.front: Which security principle integrates cloud and network security from the initial design phase?
notes.explanation: Google Cloud provides architecture blueprints and recommendations to help you apply it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement security by design: Integrate cloud security and network security considerations starting from the initial design phase of your applications and infrastructure.

notes.front: Which two Google Cloud products does the security pillar name as supporting zero trust?
notes.back: Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy.
notes.explanation: The pillar names them as products that support its never trust, always verify approach.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud supports this principle through products like Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).

notes.front: Which three Google Cloud products does the security pillar name as supporting shift-left security?
notes.back: Cloud Build, Binary Authorization and Artifact Registry.
notes.explanation: Shift-left places security controls early in the software development lifecycle, and these products are the pillar’s examples.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud supports this principle through products like Cloud Build, Binary Authorization, and Artifact Registry.

notes.front: Which security principle asks for a proactive approach built on robust fundamental measures like threat intelligence?
notes.explanation: It builds a foundation for more effective threat detection and response.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement preemptive cyber defense: Adopt a proactive approach to security by implementing robust fundamental measures like threat intelligence. This approach helps you build a foundation for more effective threat detection and response.

notes.front: Which security principle is aligned with the AI and ML perspective and Google’s Secure AI Framework?
notes.explanation: It covers developing and deploying AI systems in a responsible and secure manner.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Use AI securely and responsibly: Develop and deploy AI systems in a responsible and secure manner. The recommendations for this principle are aligned with guidance in the AI and ML perspective of the Well-Architected Framework and in Google's Secure AI Framework (SAIF).

notes.front: Which security principle uses AI capabilities, such as Gemini in Security, to improve existing security systems?
notes.explanation: It treats AI as a tool to automate remedial work and keep up security hygiene.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Use AI for security: Use AI capabilities to improve your existing security systems and processes through Gemini in Security and overall platform-security capabilities.

notes.front: Which security principle names Assured Workloads and Organization Policy Service as helping products?
notes.back: Meet regulatory, compliance, and privacy needs.
notes.explanation: It is about adhering to industry regulations, compliance standards and privacy requirements.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Meet regulatory, compliance, and privacy needs: Adhere to industry-specific regulations, compliance standards, and privacy requirements. Google Cloud helps you meet these obligations through products like Assured Workloads, Organization Policy Service, and our compliance resource center.

notes.front: Between whom is cloud security a shared responsibility, according to the security pillar?
notes.explanation: The pillar also says all stakeholders in your organisation must take a collaborative approach.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”
notes.evidence: you must recognize that cloud security is a shared responsibility between you and Google.

notes.front: A team wants only container images that passed its build checks to be deployable, and wants vulnerabilities caught in the pipeline rather than in production. Which security principle is this?
notes.choices:
A) Implement zero trust
B) Implement shift-left security
C) Implement preemptive cyber defence
D) Meet regulatory, compliance, and privacy needs
notes.choicesExplained: A governs access to resources through continuous verification. C is about threat intelligence and proactive defence. D is about regulations and standards; the controls here sit in the build pipeline.
notes.explanation: Shift-left places controls early in the development lifecycle, and names Cloud Build, Binary Authorization and Artifact Registry.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement shift-left security: Implement security controls early in the software development lifecycle. Avoid security defects before system changes are made.

notes.front: Staff reach an internal web app through a corporate network, and anyone on that network is trusted. Security wants every request checked against the user’s identity and context instead. Which principle, and which product the pillar names for it, fit?
notes.back: C: Implement zero trust, with Identity-Aware Proxy.
notes.choices:
A) Implement security by design, with architecture blueprints
B) Implement shift-left security, with Binary Authorization
C) Implement zero trust, with Identity-Aware Proxy
D) Use AI for security, with Gemini in Security
notes.choicesExplained: B controls what gets built and deployed, not who reaches the app. A is about building security in from the design phase generally. D improves security systems with AI; none of them replaces network-based trust with per-request verification.
notes.explanation: Zero trust grants access on continuous verification of trust, and the pillar names Identity-Aware Proxy as supporting it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement zero trust: Use a never trust, always verify approach, where access to resources is granted based on continuous verification of trust. Google Cloud supports this principle through products like Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).

notes.front: Zero trust and shift-left security are both security principles. What does each one govern?
notes.back: Zero trust governs access to resources through continuous verification; shift-left governs when security controls enter the development lifecycle.
notes.explanation: One is about who may reach a resource, the other about catching defects early in delivery.
notes.contrast: Zero trust: Identity-Aware Proxy. Shift-left: Cloud Build, Binary Authorization, Artifact Registry.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: where access to resources is granted based on continuous verification of trust. Google Cloud supports this principle through products like Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP). Implement shift-left security: Implement security controls early in the software development lifecycle.

notes.front: How does the reliability pillar define reliability?
notes.back: A system’s ability to consistently perform its intended functions within defined conditions and maintain uninterrupted service.
notes.explanation: Redundancy, fault-tolerant design, monitoring and automated recovery are the best practices it names.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”
notes.evidence: Reliability is a system's ability to consistently perform its intended functions within the defined conditions and maintain uninterrupted service.

notes.front: How does the reliability pillar define resilience?
notes.back: The system’s ability to withstand and recover from failures or unexpected disruptions while maintaining performance.
notes.explanation: The pillar treats resilience as a part of reliability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”
notes.evidence: As a part of reliability, resilience is the system's ability to withstand and recover from failures or unexpected disruptions, while maintaining performance.

notes.front: Which reliability focus area analyses the architecture in detail to find potential failures, bottlenecks and risks?
notes.explanation: You need to understand the components, how they interact and what could go wrong before you can mitigate it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Focus areas for reliability”
notes.evidence: Scoping: To understand your system, conduct a detailed analysis of its architecture.

notes.front: Which reliability focus area aims to reduce the impact of failures by responding appropriately and recovering efficiently?
notes.explanation: The pillar notes that even with planning and controls, failures can still occur, and that automated responses can help.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Focus areas for reliability”
notes.evidence: Response: To reduce the impact of failures, respond appropriately and recover efficiently. Automated responses can also help reduce the impact of failures. Even with planning and controls, failures can still occur.

notes.front: The first core principle of the reliability pillar is: define reliability based on {{c1::user-experience goals}}.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the nine principles the reliability pillar lists.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Define reliability based on user-experience goals

notes.front: Reliability core principle: build highly available systems through {{c1::resource redundancy}}.
notes.explanation: It sits in the pillar’s list next to taking advantage of horizontal scalability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Build highly available systems through resource redundancy

notes.front: Reliability core principle: detect potential failures by using {{c1::observability}}.
notes.explanation: It is the fifth of the pillar's nine core principles, listed after resource redundancy and horizontal scalability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Detect potential failures by using observability

notes.front: Which two kinds of recovery testing does the reliability pillar make into separate core principles?
notes.back: Testing for recovery from failures, and testing for recovery from data loss.
notes.explanation: The pillar lists them as two separate principles, next to conducting thorough postmortems.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Perform testing for recovery from failures Perform testing for recovery from data loss Conduct thorough postmortems

notes.front: Which reliability core principle comes last in the pillar's list, after the two recovery-testing principles?
notes.explanation: Postmortems turn each failure into lessons and actions, which is what the pillar's learning focus area asks for.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Perform testing for recovery from data loss Conduct thorough postmortems

notes.front: Before launch, an architect maps every component of a checkout service, how requests flow between them and what could go wrong at each step. Which reliability focus area is this?
notes.choices:
A) Observation
B) Learning
C) Response
D) Scoping
notes.choicesExplained: A is continuous monitoring of a running system. C is reacting to and recovering from failures. B is learning from failures after they happen; this work comes before launch.
notes.explanation: Scoping is the detailed analysis of the architecture to identify potential failures, bottlenecks and risks.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Reliability pillar”, “Focus areas for reliability”
notes.evidence: You need to understand the components, how they work and interact, how data and actions flow through the system, and what could go wrong. Identify potential failures, bottlenecks, and risks, which helps you to take actions to mitigate those issues.

notes.front: Which cost optimisation principle ensures cloud resources deliver measurable business value?
notes.back: Align cloud spending with business value.
notes.explanation: It does so by aligning technology spending with business objectives.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Align cloud spending with business value: Ensure that your cloud resources deliver measurable business value by aligning IT spending with business objectives.

notes.front: Which cost optimisation principle makes sure people across the organisation consider the cost impact of their decisions?
notes.back: Foster a culture of cost awareness.
notes.explanation: It also asks that they have access to the cost information they need to decide well.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Foster a culture of cost awareness: Ensure that people across your organization consider the cost impact of their decisions and activities, and ensure that they have access to the cost information required to make informed decisions.

notes.front: Which cost optimisation principle says: provision only the resources you need, and pay only for what you consume?
notes.explanation: It targets waste in what is provisioned, as opposed to the organisation’s habits or its business case.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Optimize resource usage: Provision only the resources that you need, and pay only for the resources that you consume.

notes.front: Which cost optimisation principle aims to address cost inefficiencies before they become significant problems?
notes.explanation: It relies on continuously monitoring usage and costs and adjusting proactively.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Optimize continuously: Continuously monitor your cloud resource usage and costs, and proactively make adjustments as needed to optimize your spending. This approach involves identifying and addressing potential cost inefficiencies before they become significant problems.

notes.front: Engineers at a retailer never see what their services cost, so nobody weighs cost when choosing machine sizes. Leadership wants each team to see its own spending. Which cost optimisation principle is this?
notes.back: A: Foster a culture of cost awareness.
notes.choices:
A) Foster a culture of cost awareness
B) Optimise resource usage
C) Optimise continuously
D) Align cloud spending with business value
notes.choicesExplained: D ties spending to business objectives. B is about provisioning only what is needed. C is about ongoing monitoring and adjustment; the gap here is that people lack cost information.
notes.explanation: The principle asks that people consider cost impact and have access to the cost information needed to decide.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Foster a culture of cost awareness: Ensure that people across your organization consider the cost impact of their decisions and activities, and ensure that they have access to the cost information required to make informed decisions.

notes.front: The performance optimisation pillar’s first core principle is: {{c1::plan resource allocation}}.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the pillar’s four core principles.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: are mapped to the following core principles: Plan resource allocation Take advantage of elasticity Promote modular design Continuously monitor and improve performance

notes.front: Performance optimisation core principle: take advantage of {{c1::elasticity}}.
notes.explanation: It is the second of the pillar’s four core principles, after planning resource allocation.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Plan resource allocation Take advantage of elasticity Promote modular design

notes.front: Performance optimisation core principle: promote {{c1::modular design}}.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the pillar’s four principles.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Take advantage of elasticity Promote modular design Continuously monitor and improve performance

notes.front: Which performance optimisation principle reflects that performance optimisation is a continuous process, not a one-time activity?
notes.explanation: The pillar describes performance optimisation as an ongoing cycle.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: Performance optimization is a continuous process, not a one-time activity.

notes.front: What are the four stages of the performance optimisation cycle?
notes.back: Define requirements; design and deploy; monitor and analyse; optimise.
notes.explanation: After optimising, you keep monitoring, reassessing requirements and adjusting resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: The performance optimization process is an ongoing cycle that includes the following stages: Define requirements: Define granular performance requirements for each layer of the application stack before you design and develop your applications.

notes.front: Is performance always traded against cost, according to the performance pillar?
notes.back: No. There can be a trade-off, but optimising performance can sometimes reduce costs.
notes.explanation: Autoscaling keeps performance predictable under load and removes unused resources when load is low.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: The performance optimization process can involve a trade-off between performance and cost. However, optimizing performance can sometimes help you reduce costs.

notes.front: Before writing any code, an architect sets a latency target for the web layer, the application layer and the database separately. Which stage of the performance optimisation cycle is this?
notes.choices:
A) Optimise
B) Design and deploy
C) Monitor and analyse
D) Define requirements
notes.choicesExplained: B uses elastic, scalable design patterns to meet the requirements. C watches logs, traces, metrics and alerts once running. A rightsizes and redesigns as the application evolves.
notes.explanation: That stage defines granular performance requirements for each layer before design and development.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Performance optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: Define requirements: Define granular performance requirements for each layer of the application stack before you design and develop your applications.

notes.front: The sustainability pillar’s first core principle is: use {{c1::regions that consume low-carbon energy}}.
notes.explanation: Region choice is the first of the pillar’s eight principles.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Sustainability pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Use regions that consume low-carbon energy Optimize AI and ML workloads for energy efficiency

notes.front: Under the shared responsibility model for sustainability, what is Google responsible for and what are you responsible for?
notes.back: Google: sustainability of Google Cloud. You: sustainability in the cloud, by making your workloads energy efficient.
notes.explanation: Google’s share covers the energy efficiency and water stewardship of its data centres, infrastructure and core services.
notes.contrast: Customer examples: right-size resources, use serverless services that scale to zero, manage data lifecycles.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Sustainability pillar”, “Shared responsibility and shared fate”
notes.evidence: Google is responsible for the sustainability of Google Cloud, which means the energy efficiency and water stewardship of our data centers, infrastructure, and core services.

notes.front: A company’s cloud workloads keep idle development virtual machines running every weekend. Under the pillar’s shared responsibility model, whose job is it to fix this?
notes.back: D: The customer’s, as part of sustainability in the cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Google’s, as part of sustainability of the cloud
B) Nobody’s: idle machines use no energy
C) The hardware supplier’s
D) The customer’s, as part of sustainability in the cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A covers Google’s data centres, infrastructure and core services, not your running machines. B is wrong: running resources consume energy. C is not a party in the model, which is between Google and the customer.
notes.explanation: The customer is responsible for optimising its workloads to be energy efficient, for example by right-sizing resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Sustainability pillar”, “Shared responsibility and shared fate”
notes.evidence: You, the customer, are responsible for sustainability in the cloud, which means optimizing your workloads to be energy efficient. For example, you can right-size resources, use serverless services that scale to zero, and manage data lifecycles effectively.

notes.front: What is a deployment archetype?
notes.back: An abstract, provider-independent model used as the foundation for application-specific deployment architectures.
notes.explanation: Each archetype specifies a combination of zones, regions, on-premises data centres or other clouds where the application can run.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “What is a deployment archetype?”
notes.evidence: A deployment archetype is an abstract, provider-independent model that you use as the foundation to build application-specific deployment architectures that meet your business and technical requirements.

notes.front: Which six deployment archetypes does Google Cloud’s guide describe?
notes.back: Zonal, regional, multi-regional, global, hybrid and multicloud.
notes.explanation: The first four are the basic archetypes; hybrid and multicloud build on one of them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”
notes.evidence: This guide describes six deployment archetypes—zonal, regional, multi-regional, global, hybrid, and multicloud

notes.front: In which deployment archetype does the application run within a single Google Cloud zone?
notes.explanation: Its design consideration is downtime during zone outages; a passive replica in another zone of the same region helps business continuity.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Zonal”
notes.evidence: Your application runs within a single Google Cloud zone

notes.front: In which deployment archetype does the application run independently in two or more zones within one Google Cloud region?
notes.explanation: It suits highly available applications for users in one geographic area, but still goes down in a region outage.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Regional”
notes.evidence: Your application runs independently in two or more zones within a single Google Cloud region

notes.front: In which deployment archetype can routing policies of the domain name system send traffic to regional load balancers in two or more regions?
notes.explanation: Its design considerations are cross-region data transfer and replication costs, and operational complexity.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Multi-regional”
notes.evidence: Your application runs independently in multiple zones across two or more Google Cloud regions. You can use DNS routing policies to route incoming traffic to the regional load balancers.

notes.front: In which deployment archetype does a global anycast load balancer send traffic to the region nearest the user?
notes.explanation: The stack can be globally distributed or regionally isolated, and other components such as the database can also be global.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Global”
notes.evidence: A global anycast load balancer distributes traffic to the region that's nearest to the user. Other components of the application stack can also be global, such as the database, cache, and object store.

notes.front: In which deployment archetype are some parts of the application in Google Cloud and others on-premises?
notes.explanation: Listed use cases include a disaster recovery site for on-premises workloads and progressive migration of legacy applications.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Hybrid”
notes.evidence: Certain parts of your application are deployed in Google Cloud, and other parts run on-premises

notes.front: In which deployment archetype are some parts of the application in Google Cloud and others on other cloud platforms?
notes.explanation: Its design considerations include the cost of redundant resources and cross-cloud network traffic.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Multicloud”
notes.evidence: Some parts of your application are deployed in Google Cloud, and other parts are deployed in other cloud platforms

notes.front: Why can hybrid and multicloud be called composite deployment archetypes?
notes.back: Their cloud topology is based on one of the basic archetypes: zonal, regional, multi-regional or global.
notes.explanation: So choosing hybrid still leaves you to choose a basic archetype for the Google Cloud part.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “What is a deployment archetype?”
notes.evidence: the hybrid and multicloud deployment archetypes can be considered as composite deployment archetypes that include one of the basic archetypes.

notes.front: A Compute Engine virtual machine has a zonal location scope. Does that force a zonal deployment archetype?
notes.back: No. Spreading virtual machines across several zones gives a highly available architecture based on the regional archetype.
notes.explanation: Location scope is one resource’s availability boundary; the archetype describes where the whole application runs.
notes.contrast: Location scope: availability boundary of a single resource.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “What is a deployment archetype?”
notes.evidence: For example, the location scope of a Compute Engine VM is zonal. This means that if the Google Cloud zone in which a VM is provisioned has an outage, the availability of the VM is affected. However, by distributing VMs across multiple zones, you can build a highly available architecture that's based on the regional deployment archetype.

notes.front: What outage takes down each of the zonal and regional archetypes, and what does the guide suggest for continuity?
notes.back: Zonal: a zone outage; keep a passive replica in another zone. Regional: a region outage; back up to another region.
notes.explanation: The guide lists the outage each archetype cannot survive as its first design consideration.
notes.contrast: Regional also adds the cost and effort of redundant resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Regional”
notes.evidence: Design considerations Downtime during region outages. For business continuity, you can back up the application and data to another region.

notes.front: An internal expenses app is used only by staff in one country. It must survive the loss of a single zone, and the owners care more about cost than about surviving a whole-region outage. Which archetype fits best?
notes.choices:
A) Zonal
B) Global
C) Multi-regional
D) Regional
notes.choicesExplained: A fails with a single zone outage. C and B protect against region loss but add cross-region transfer and replication costs the owners do not want.
notes.explanation: The guide’s own trade-off: for an internal app in one geography you might prioritise cost over availability and choose regional.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “What is a deployment archetype?”
notes.evidence: But for an internal application that's used by employees in a single geographical region, you might prioritize cost over availability and, therefore, choose the regional deployment archetype.

notes.front: A manufacturer keeps its production systems in its own data centre but wants a recovery site it can fail over to in Google Cloud. Which archetype describes this?
notes.choices:
A) Hybrid
B) Global
C) Zonal
D) Multicloud
notes.choicesExplained: D mixes Google Cloud with other cloud platforms, not an on-premises site. B and C describe only the Google Cloud topology, which a hybrid design still contains.
notes.explanation: The guide lists a disaster recovery site for on-premises workloads as a hybrid use case.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Hybrid”
notes.evidence: Use cases Disaster recovery (DR) site for on-premises workloads. On-premises development for cloud applications. Progressive migration to the cloud for legacy applications.

notes.front: A mobile game has players on every continent and wants them routed to the nearest region, with a single globally replicated database behind the stacks. Which archetype matches?
notes.choices:
A) Regional
B) Global
C) Hybrid
D) Zonal
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the app in one region. C places parts on-premises. D keeps the app in a single zone; none routes worldwide users to the nearest region.
notes.explanation: In the global archetype a global anycast load balancer sends users to the nearest region, and components such as the database can be global.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Global”
notes.evidence: All the application stacks use a single, globally replicated database.

notes.front: A batch simulation runs on licence-restricted software, needs very low latency between its nodes and can tolerate downtime. Which archetype does the guide’s list of use cases point to?
notes.choices:
A) Regional
B) Zonal
C) Multi-regional
D) Multicloud
notes.choicesExplained: A and C add redundancy the workload does not need and put nodes further apart. D spreads parts across cloud providers, which suits none of these needs.
notes.explanation: Low-latency links between components, licence-restricted software and no need for high availability are all zonal use cases.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Zonal”
notes.evidence: Applications that don't need high availability. Low-latency networking between application components. Migrating commodity workloads. Applications that use license-restricted software.

notes.front: A bank runs its main platform in Google Cloud and keeps a standby copy with another cloud provider for recovery. Which archetype is this?
notes.choices:
A) Hybrid
B) Global
C) Multi-regional
D) Multicloud
notes.choicesExplained: A involves on-premises, not another cloud. C and B stay within Google Cloud regions.
notes.explanation: Using Google Cloud as the primary site with another cloud as a recovery site is a listed multicloud use case.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud deployment archetypes”, “Multicloud”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud as the primary site and another cloud as a DR site.

notes.front: Part of a firm’s order system stays on-premises while the rest moves to Google Cloud. A colleague says the Well-Architected Framework does not apply because the system is not cloud-native. Is the colleague right?
notes.back: D: No. The framework is relevant to migrated workloads and hybrid deployments as well.
notes.choices:
A) Yes. It covers only applications built for the cloud
B) No, but only its security pillar applies
C) Yes, until the whole system has been migrated
D) No. It is relevant to migrated workloads and hybrid deployments as well
notes.choicesExplained: A and C contradict the stated scope, which includes migrated and hybrid workloads. B is wrong because nothing limits hybrid systems to one pillar.
notes.explanation: Its stated scope covers applications built for the cloud, workloads migrated from on-premises, hybrid and multi-cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”
notes.evidence: The Well-Architected Framework is relevant to applications built for the cloud and for workloads migrated from on-premises to Google Cloud, hybrid cloud deployments, and multi-cloud environments.

notes.front: A design review asks whether a new health-records system meets national data-protection regulations and privacy expectations. Which pillar of the framework does this question belong to?
notes.choices:
A) Security, privacy, and compliance
B) Reliability
C) Cost optimisation
D) Operational excellence
notes.choicesExplained: D covers deploying, operating, monitoring and managing workloads. B covers resilience and availability. C covers business value of spending; none covers regulation and privacy.
notes.explanation: That pillar covers designing for privacy and aligning with regulatory requirements and standards.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Security, privacy, and compliance Maximize the security of your data and workloads in the cloud, design for privacy, and align with regulatory requirements and standards.
